newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr shivers in shadow of RBA board.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr shivers in shadow of RBA board.

text.p: The Australian dollar gave an edgy performance Tuesday as the market fretted over the risk of an imminent rate cut, but such was the uncertainty that dealers felt it better to take cover than take positions.

The currency eased through the morning as the bond market worked itself up into a lather on speculation today's monthly meeting of the Reserve Bank board would result in a policy easing as early as Wednesday morning.
Dollar demand linked to a dual currency issue and modestly firm retail sales and building data helped steady nerves, but nothing and nobody was certain until 9.30 am tomorrow.
By 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) Tuesday the local dollar was hovering at US$0.7910/15 after bouncing from a US$0.7898/03 morning low, but was still short of Monday's late US$0.7930/35.
It was soggy on the crosses, sagging to 87.71/81 yen from 88.24/34 late Monday and to 1.2035/47 marks from 1.2067/79. In trade weighted terms it eased to 58.4 from a 58.5 close.
Traders said Japanese profit-taking on recent strong US$/yen gains had been largely behind the pullback, with the U.S. unit lapsing to 110.99/03 yen from 111.35/40 late here Monday.
This was the currency's twelfth successive session in the US$0.7855/7945 range, but all that could be changed by the RBA.

The majority of analysts here are tipping the RBA to ease again before year end, but believe the board will first want to see its expectations of slowing inflation and wages growth confirmed by third quarter data out late this month.

Few, however, would completely rule out the chance of an immediate easing so tension was set to be high ahead of the bank's regular money market operation at 9.30 am (2330 GMT) Wednesday in the assumption it would follow the pattern of the last cut on July 31.
If no move came then, the market would probably assume a cut was off the agenda until late October, dealers said.
Such an outcome would likely see a relieved dollar test the US$0.7945 resistance peak from last week with a prospect of reaching 80 cents on renewed samurai demand from Japan.

If the RBA were to cut rates -- almost certainly by 0.5 point to 6.5 percent -- it would shrink the local currency's yield premium over the U.S. dollar to unappetising levels. That would probably ensure a break of US$0.7855 support with a risk of testing the pivotal US$0.7810 chart level near term.
The money market appreciated the risk and the 90-day bank bill future contract for December remained at 93.40, implying an interest rate of 6.60 percent against the current 7.0 percent.
Today's domestic economic data, as with most other figures recently, contained enough strong and soft points to support arguments both for an immediate easing and for a pause.

Retail sales rose 1.1 percent in August compared to forecasts of a 1.2 percent decline, but the upbeat message was diluted by a sharp downward revision to July's rise to 1.0 percent from an original 2.4 percent.

The figures were either very promising or masked a weaker underlying performance depending on who you talked to, but all had to agree that consumer spending was set to make a healthy contribution to Q3 GDP growth even if September sales were soft.
Also out were building approvals data for August and again there was plenty for bulls and bears to latch onto.
Approvals rose 1.6 percent compared to forecasts of a 1.0 percent gain which suggested that July's 8.1 percent jump may have been a turning point in the housing market's long fall.
However, analysts noted private sector house approvals -- the largest part of the market -- remained weak and total building approvals were still close to 13-year lows.
Given all these ambiguities it was hard to see the data pushing the RBA one way or the other, analysts concluded.
